subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage:
The power went out at nine, the night before the school council speeches, so Mahima practised by candlelight in the room she shared with her older sister. Zainab listened from the top bunk, then said, "The middle part is boring. And you say 'basically' about eleven times."
Mahima's face went hot. She blew out the candle a little too hard. "Wow. Thanks."
"What? You asked."
In the dark, Mahima counted her breaths. Then she said, "When you say it like that, it sounds like the whole speech is bad. Is it?"
Zainab was quiet for a moment. "No. The opening is really good. I just meant the middle drags."
"Then say that part too, okay? It helps me hear the rest."
Mahima relit the candle, crossed out the extra 'basically's and cut the middle paragraph in half. Zainab climbed down to hold the page steady.

qa.q: Why was Mahima practising by candlelight?
qa.a: The power went out at nine, the night before the school council speeches.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when Zainab called the middle part boring, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt stung and hurt: her face went hot, she blew out the candle a little too hard and said a flat "Wow. Thanks."

qa.q: Which step helped Mahima most, and why?
qa.a: She told Zainab how the words sounded and asked if the whole speech was bad. That let her keep the useful points about the middle and the 'basically's without carrying the sting.

qa.q: How does Zainab see her own comment?
qa.a: Zainab thought she was just being honest because Mahima asked. Once she heard how it landed, she said the opening was good and came down to help.

grounding: Shows a teen hurt by her sister's blunt feedback telling her how the words land and pulling the honest point apart from the tone.

passage:
Inside the kitchen cupboard of their shared flat in Lisbon, Noa kept a sticky note: Dalia – rent top-up, bus pass, concert ticket. She had never meant it as a bill; it was just so she wouldn't forget.
On Thursday Dalia leaned in the doorway. "Tiny favour? My card's being weird again. Could you cover the groceries? I'll pay you back Friday, promise."
Noa was already reaching for her wallet. Then she glanced at the note and noticed that every Friday on it had come and gone. The same week, Dalia had posted photos from a weekend away at the coast.
Noa's stomach tightened. She liked being the one people could count on. "I can't this time," she said, her voice wobbling. "And I'd like us to sit down and go through the list first."
Dalia rolled her eyes. "Seriously? I thought we were friends."
"We are. That's why I'm saying it."

qa.q: Where did Noa keep the sticky note?
qa.a: Inside the kitchen cupboard of their shared flat in Lisbon.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling when she said "I can't this time"?
qa.a: She felt anxious and torn: her stomach tightened and her voice wobbled, because she liked being someone people could count on but saw that every promised Friday had passed.

qa.q: What could Noa do next to protect both her kindness and herself?
qa.a: She could hold the talk about the list, stay friendly but firm, and if Dalia keeps asking, talk it through with someone she trusts before agreeing to help again.

qa.q: Why might Dalia react with an eye-roll?
qa.a: Dalia is used to Noa saying yes, so a no feels like a change in the friendship; being asked about the list may also embarrass her.

grounding: Shows a generous young adult noticing that her help is being taken for granted and starting to set a limit.

passage:
Last month Nazia asked me to run the cultural fest stall with her for all three days. The old me would have said yes, then stayed up panicking over unfinished lab reports.
This time I said, "You're right that the stall needs two people, and I'll make the posters this weekend. But I can't do the three days." No long speech, no five sorries.
She stared at me. "Seriously, Deepika? I was counting on you." Her voice went flat.
For an hour afterwards I kept typing apology messages and deleting them. Her disappointment felt like proof that I'd been cruel. But I hadn't been. I had agreed to what I could do and been honest about the rest of my week.
The posters came out bright yellow. Nazia replied with a thumbs-up, a bit cool. By Friday we were sharing chips in the canteen again, and I had finished two lab reports.

qa.q: What did Deepika offer to do for the stall?
qa.a: Deepika offered to make the posters that weekend.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel after saying no, and what shows it?
qa.a: Deepika felt guilty and uneasy, typing apology messages for an hour and deleting them, because Nazia's disappointment felt like proof of being cruel.

qa.q: What made Deepika's answer kind but firm?
qa.a: Deepika agreed with what was true, that the stall needed two people, offered real help with posters, and declined the three days without a long apology.

qa.q: How might Nazia have seen the answer at first, and later?
qa.a: At first Nazia felt let down because she was counting on Deepika. By Friday she was sharing chips in the canteen, which suggests the friendship could take an honest no.

grounding: Shows a young adult saying a warm, clear no without over-apologising and accepting a friend's disappointment as not the same as cruelty.

passage:
Team lead's notes, Friday.
This week I watched how the team really runs. When the client moved the deadline, Usha stayed late to rebuild the slides for Chandrika, who was off sick. On Wednesday Usha quietly fixed two broken formulas in my own sheet and never mentioned it.
In the review meeting the slides were praised, and Usha's name came up nowhere. She smiled and kept taking notes.
When I asked her about the new onboarding project, she said, "Sure, happy to." Then I looked at the board: she already had four open tasks. I felt uncomfortable that I had nearly added a fifth.
What I did next: I moved two of her tasks to Imran and to myself. I named her work on the slides in the team email. I also put her forward for the review round in March, and asked her directly what she wants to grow into. She took a long time to answer.

qa.q: How many open tasks did Usha already have on the board?
qa.a: Usha already had four open tasks.

qa.q: What was the team lead feeling on seeing the board, and why?
qa.a: The team lead felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed at nearly adding a fifth task to Usha's four, after seeing how much of her work went unnoticed.

qa.q: Which of the team lead's steps shares the load fairly?
qa.a: Moving two of Usha's tasks to Imran and to the team lead spreads the work, and naming her in the team email and the review round shares the credit.

qa.q: What might it be like for Usha when her name is missing from the review meeting?
qa.a: Usha smiled and kept taking notes, but going unnamed again may leave her feeling invisible; her long pause when asked what she wants suggests she is not used to being asked.

grounding: Shows a team lead noticing an always-helpful colleague being overloaded and uncredited, and sharing out both the work and the recognition.

passage:
Monday: The pressure cooker whistled and Anjali screamed and grabbed her mother Manjula's leg. She sobbed long after the kitchen went quiet while Manjula held her and hummed.
Wednesday: Before the whistle, Manjula picked her up. "Loud sound coming." Anjali buried her face and cried a little, then settled sooner in her arms.
Saturday: At the first hiss, Anjali ran to Manjula herself, hands over her ears. Then she peeked out and pointed at the cooker.

qa.q: What made Anjali scream on Monday?
qa.a: The pressure cooker whistled.

qa.q: How was Anjali feeling on Monday, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was frightened and upset: she screamed, grabbed Manjula's leg and sobbed long after the kitchen went quiet.

qa.q: What did Manjula try on Wednesday that helped?
qa.a: She picked Anjali up before the whistle and said, "Loud sound coming," so the noise came with warning and comfort.

qa.q: What is it like for Manjula when Anjali takes so long to settle?
qa.a: It takes patience; Manjula keeps holding and humming instead of scolding, and by Saturday she sees Anjali come to her and even peek at the cooker.

grounding: Shows a toddler who cries hard at a loud noise and settles slowly, and how steady comfort over several days helps.

passage:
Nap time at the Little Stars crèche. The blinds were down, but Jomon sat up on his mat.
"Aunty Chandrika, what if a storm comes?"
"Then we'll stay inside here. It's a strong building."
"What if Appa is late?"
Chandrika knelt beside him. "What happens after nap?"
"Snack," he whispered.
"Then?"
"Painting. Then songs."
"And then Appa comes. Every day, after songs."
Jomon lay back down, still holding his blanket tight. A minute later he asked, "What if a monster—"
"Monsters don't come to the crèche," she said softly, "but I'll sit right here." She stayed, patting his back, until his breathing slowed.

qa.q: What comes after snack in Jomon's day?
qa.a: Painting, then songs.

qa.q: What was Jomon worried about at nap time?
qa.a: He felt scared that a storm might come or that Appa would be late; he kept sitting up and holding his blanket tight.

qa.q: Why did going through the day's order help Jomon?
qa.a: Saying snack, painting, songs, then Appa gave him a steady picture of what comes next, which calmed him more than being told not to worry.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see Jomon's questions?
qa.a: She treats them as real worries, not naughtiness, so she answers calmly and sits beside him until he settles.

grounding: Shows a young child with many what-if worries being soothed by calm answers and a predictable routine.

passage:
Come, Gargi, sit. You think your Nilesh Mama was always this calm? When I was about your age, my stomach twisted every test morning. Once, in Class 4, I read "Tuesday" as "Thursday" aloud and the whole class laughed. For days I replayed it at night and felt hot in the face all over again.
My mother didn't tell me to stop being silly. She sat on my bed and asked, "Where in your body is the worry?" I pointed at my stomach. "What is it saying?" "That I'll forget everything."
Then we made a small plan. The night before a test, revise just one page. In the morning, three slow breaths at the school gate. The first time it barely helped. By the half-yearly exams the ache came smaller, and I could say, "That's my nervous feeling."
So, what is your stomach saying about tomorrow's maths test?

qa.q: What did young Nilesh read wrongly in Class 4?
qa.a: He read "Tuesday" as "Thursday" aloud.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel in the days after the class laughed?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed for a long time; he kept replaying it at night and felt hot in the face all over again.

qa.q: What choice by his mother helped young Nilesh, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked where the worry sat and what it was saying instead of calling him silly, then made a small plan with him, so he learned to name the feeling and take one step at a time.

qa.q: How might his mother have seen those test mornings?
qa.a: She seemed to take his stomach aches seriously as worry, not fuss, and chose to sit with him and plan rather than brush it off.

grounding: Shows an uncle telling how, as a child, his test-morning stomach aches and replayed embarrassment eased by naming feelings and taking small steps.

passage:
Class teacher's note on Pallavi, Class 10, for my own record.
Monday: Pallavi snapped at Payal over a borrowed pen, then apologised in a whisper.
Tuesday: after the unit test marks, she kept her head down and said, "I'm just bad at everything."
Thursday: laughing with her group, fine in class, and she volunteered to read aloud.
Friday: she asked to skip the class photo because her hair "looked terrible".
Swings like these are very common at this age, and she is still coming to school, finishing work and spending time with friends. I asked her to stay back for two minutes and said, "Some weeks feel up and down. That's allowed." She nodded, eyes wet.
I told her the school counsellor is there if the feelings start getting in the way of sleep, eating or coming to school, and that I'm here too. I will keep watching gently and mention it to her mother at the parent meeting.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi want to skip the class photo?
qa.a: She said her hair "looked terrible".

qa.q: How was Pallavi feeling after the unit test marks, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt low and doubtful about herself; she kept her head down and said, "I'm just bad at everything."

qa.q: How did the teacher support Pallavi without making it a big deal?
qa.a: The teacher spoke to her for two minutes, said up-and-down weeks are allowed, and named the counsellor and the teacher as people to go to if it starts getting in the way of daily life.

qa.q: What might Payal have felt when Pallavi snapped at her over a pen?
qa.a: Payal may have been hurt or surprised, but the whispered apology probably helped her see it was about Pallavi's mood, not about her.

grounding: Shows a teacher noting a teen's swings between irritation, worry and low confidence, treating them as common while watching for signs they disrupt daily life.

passage:
The film started at six, and it was already 5:40 when Jyoti's phone buzzed under the bus shelter. Rain was hammering the roof.
Jasleen: sorry sorry I can't come. I think I read Mehak's message wrong and now it'll be awkward
Jyoti sighed. It was the third time this month. Her first thought was to type "you always do this". She deleted it.
Instead she wrote: "Okay. The film's on again Sunday afternoon. I'll save you a seat either way."
She added: "Want me to look at Mehak's message with you after?"
The bus came, and Jyoti watched the film alone, a little disappointed. Afterwards she called. Jasleen read the message aloud; it was only "k". "She sends 'k' to everyone," Jyoti said. Jasleen laughed shakily.
On Sunday, Jasleen came. She held Jyoti's sleeve at the door, but she came.

qa.q: What time did the film start?
qa.a: The film started at six.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when Jasleen cancelled, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and a little disappointed, since it was the third time that month, but she deleted "you always do this" and wrote a calm reply instead.

qa.q: Which of Jyoti's choices helped Jasleen most?
qa.a: Offering the Sunday show and a saved seat "either way", then calling to look at Mehak's message together, showed steady support without blame.

qa.q: What might it be like for Jasleen to cancel again?
qa.a: Jasleen seems embarrassed and caught in overthinking the message; hearing a patient reply instead of anger probably made it easier for her to come on Sunday.

grounding: Shows a teen staying patient and consistent with a friend who overthinks messages and cancels plans, which helps the friend feel less alone.

passage:
Coach's notebook, district relay week.
Aadhya came to practice on Tuesday pale and quiet. "My heart's going crazy. What if I drop the baton again?" she said. Last year she did, once.
I didn't tell her it was nothing. I said, "Your heart's telling you this matters. It's a signal to slow down, not a sign you'll fail." We walked one easy lap while she named three worries out loud. Ankita, her partner on the handover, listened and said, "I worry about that too."
We made a small plan: an early night before the meet, a short jog in the morning, and ten slow handovers with Ankita instead of fifty fast ones.
She ran well on Saturday, still shaky at the start line.
Afterwards she told me the worry follows her at home too, most nights. I thanked her for telling me, and with her permission I called her mother that evening so they could talk to the school counsellor together.

qa.q: How many slow handovers did Aadhya plan to practise with Ankita?
qa.a: Ten slow handovers.

qa.q: What was Aadhya worried about on Tuesday?
qa.a: She felt anxious that she might drop the baton again; she was pale and quiet and said her heart was going crazy.

qa.q: What did the coach do well when Aadhya said the worry follows her most nights?
qa.a: The coach thanked her and, with her permission, called her mother that same evening so they could talk to the school counsellor together, since ongoing worry deserves more support.

qa.q: How might Ankita's words have affected Aadhya?
qa.a: Hearing "I worry about that too" from her handover partner likely made Aadhya feel less alone and less ashamed of her nerves.

grounding: Shows a coach helping a teen treat racing nerves as a signal, using sleep, movement, naming worries and sharing, and involving a counsellor for ongoing distress.
